executive_summary: The file is 19 lines of detection logic that decides reportability, with no obligation reference, no rationale, no record of its own decision, no tests and no change-control history. The threshold value 10000 is numerically consistent with the US CTR trigger and the > boundary is correct against the rule as written, but numeric coincidence is not governance: nothing in the artifact records why the number is that number, who owns it, when it was set, when it is next reviewed, or what currency and unit it is expressed in, and any caller can silently override it through the limit keyword argument. Three regulatory-substance defects sit underneath that. Cash-in and cash-out are summed into one total rather than aggregated separately. Aggregation is scoped to an account rather than to a person, which is the entity the aggregation rule names. Nothing restricts the input to transactions in currency. Each of those changes which days are reported, in both directions. The function returns a bare bool, so no BSA examiner or internal tester can reconstruct why any given account did or did not alert on any given day. Data handling is clean and is recorded as such. Ravi owns the engineering form of the aggregation defect and of the magic constant; this pack addresses only the regulatory consequence and does not restate his code findings.
developer_guidance: Forward-looking, for whoever next touches detection logic in this project. (1) A threshold is a controlled parameter, not a literal. Put it in a versioned configuration object carrying value, currency, unit, rationale, owner, effective date, tuning date and next-review date, and have the code read it rather than embed it. A number that can only be changed by a code deploy but can also be overridden per call has the drawbacks of both. (2) Write the obligation into the code at the point the rule is expressed. One comment naming the regulation, the section and the register id costs a line and removes an entire class of audit finding. (3) Make every detection decision self-evidencing. Return or emit a record carrying the inputs used, the computed aggregate, the threshold value and version applied, the entity and window evaluated, and a timestamp, for negative decisions as well as positive ones. A rule that cannot explain a non-alert cannot be tested below the line. (4) Encode aggregation entity, direction and window as named, explicit parameters. Where a rule says "by or on behalf of any person" and "cash in or cash out" and "one business day", each of those three should be visible in the signature rather than implied by a docstring. (5) Build the true-positive and false-positive test pair as you build the rule, including the exact boundary case, because the boundary is where the rule text and the code most often disagree.

title: No traceable link from the reportability decision to any regulatory obligation
standard: CLAUDE.md section 4 (traceable link alert to logic to regulatory obligation) and Definition of Done, Traceable item (requirement to design to code to test to obligation). Obligation the code appears to serve, TO-VERIFY: 31 CFR 1010.311, currency transaction reports, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.311
problem: All 19 lines were read. The file names no regulation, no rule section, no requirement id, no internal scenario id and no specification. The words reportable and reporting limit appear at lines 1, 18 and 19 without ever saying reportable to whom, under what, or why. check_citations.py run against the file returns 0 verified and 0 to-verify citations, which mechanically confirms there is no pinpoint anywhere in it. No RTM exists in the project. There is no git repository, so there is also no commit message, no pull request and no approval record that could carry the link instead.
likely_cause: The obligation was obvious to the author at the time of writing and was held as tribal knowledge rather than written down. A 19-line utility reads as too small to need a citation, which is exactly how a regulatory link goes missing from a control that carries one.
impact: The control is not audit defensible. An examiner or internal auditor asking what obligation this implements cannot get an answer from the artifact, and the firm cannot demonstrate that its currency-transaction monitoring is mapped to the rule it is meant to satisfy. It also blocks impact analysis: if the underlying threshold or aggregation rule changes, nothing identifies this file as affected. The minimum acceptable trail is three things, none of which exist: a comment at the threshold and at the decision function naming the regulation and section, a requirement id in an RTM row linking requirement to this code to its tests to that obligation, and a register entry recording the pinpoint as human-verified.

fix.diff:
DAILY_LIMIT = 10000
+ # Obligation: 31 CFR 1010.311 (CTR filing) with aggregation per 31 CFR 1010.313(b).
+ # Requirement: REQ-CTR-001. Register id: to be added after human verification of both pinpoints.

  def is_reportable(transactions, limit=DAILY_LIMIT):
-     """True when the day's aggregate breaches the reporting limit."""
+     """True when a person's same-day currency total exceeds the CTR threshold.
+
+     Implements REQ-CTR-001. Obligation: 31 CFR 1010.311, aggregation 31 CFR 1010.313(b).
+     TO-VERIFY: both pinpoints pending confirmation against the primary source.
+     """
fix.why: It puts the obligation where the logic is, so the link survives refactoring and is visible to the next reader without external context. The RTM row then makes the same link machine-checkable by validate_rtm, which turns an advisory expectation into an enforced one. Marking the pinpoints TO-VERIFY records them honestly as unconfirmed rather than asserting them as decided fact.

title: DAILY_LIMIT is not a governable control: no rationale, owner, date or review cycle, and any caller can override it silently
standard: CLAUDE.md section 4: no hard-coded thresholds without a comment recording rationale and tuning date; detection rules must be explainable and auditable. FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual expectation that monitoring thresholds are documented, owned and periodically reviewed, TO-VERIFY: https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/manual
problem: Line 6 is a bare module constant with no comment of any kind. There is no recorded rationale for the value, no named owner, no tuning or effective date, no next-review date and no version identifier. Line 17 then exposes the same value as a default keyword argument, so any caller can pass a different limit and the module will use it without recording that it did. The value can therefore only be changed globally by a code deploy, while being silently overridable per call. It has the rigidity of a constant and the ungovernability of a runtime input at the same time.
likely_cause: A familiar number was written inline because it looked self-evident, and the keyword argument was added for test convenience without anyone deciding whether the threshold is a fixed control or a caller-supplied input. The question of which it is was never posed, so it was never governed.
impact: Answering the question this review was asked to answer: as written, the threshold is NOT defensible, independently of whether 10000 is the right number. A control whose value carries no rationale, no owner and no review date cannot be evidenced as governed, and one that a caller can override without leaving a record cannot be evidenced as applied. At examination the firm can state what the code contains but cannot demonstrate who set it, on what basis, when it was last reviewed, or that the value in force on any past date was the value in the file.

fix.diff:
- DAILY_LIMIT = 10000
+ # CTR reporting threshold. Value: 10000. Currency: USD. Unit: whole dollars.
+ # Rationale: statutory CTR trigger, 31 CFR 1010.311 (more than $10,000). TO-VERIFY.
+ # Owner: <named BSA officer>. Set: <YYYY-MM-DD>. Last tuned: <YYYY-MM-DD>.
+ # Next review: <YYYY-MM-DD>. Threshold version: v1.
+ CTR_THRESHOLD_USD = 10000

- def is_reportable(transactions, limit=DAILY_LIMIT):
+ def is_reportable(transactions, threshold=None):
+     """threshold overrides the governed value; every override is recorded in the
+     decision record (see CMP-04) so the applied value is always reconstructable."""
fix.why: Moving the governance metadata next to the value makes the control self-documenting, which is what section 4 asks for and what an examiner reads first. Naming the currency and unit in the identifier removes the ambiguity CMP-06 raises. Recording any override in the decision record means the applied threshold is always evidenced, so a caller-supplied value stops being an invisible change to the control. The stronger form, which this project should move to, is a versioned threshold configuration read at runtime rather than a literal at all.

title: Aggregation does not match the CTR aggregation rule: cash-in and cash-out are summed together, the entity is the account rather than the person, and non-currency transactions are not excluded
location: alert_threshold_check.py:9-14 (aggregate_daily), :10 (docstring claiming one account), :19 (comparison over that total)
standard: 31 CFR 1010.313(b), aggregation of multiple currency transactions, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.313 . Filing obligation 31 CFR 1010.311, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.311 . As this reviewer understands the rule text and subject to that verification, it treats multiple transactions as one where the institution has knowledge they are by or on behalf of any person and result in either cash in OR cash out totalling more than $10,000 during any one business day.
problem: Line 13 performs total = total + txn["amount"] over every element of the input with no direction, entity or instrument test. Three consequences follow from the source as read. First, cash in and cash out are combined into one number, where the rule tests each direction separately. If amounts are unsigned, $9,000 in and $9,000 out reads as $18,000 and reports a day that is not reportable. If amounts are signed, the same day nets to $0 and a genuinely reportable day can be missed. The code does not reveal which convention applies, and neither does the docstring. Second, line 10 scopes the aggregate to one account, while the rule aggregates by or on behalf of any person; a person operating several accounts stays below the line on each. Third, nothing restricts the input to transactions in currency, so non-cash activity can inflate the total. Ravi owns the engineering form of the missing date and account filtering; this finding is the separate regulatory-completeness consequence and does not restate his.
likely_cause: The rule was implemented from the remembered headline, a daily total over ten thousand dollars, rather than from the aggregation provision's actual text. The three qualifiers that matter, direction, person and currency, all live in that text and none of them survived into the code.
impact: Reporting completeness is wrong in both directions and the direction of the error cannot be predicted from the artifact. Under-reporting risks failure to file a required CTR. Over-reporting generates filings that are not required, which wastes investigative capacity and degrades the quality of the firm's reporting. Because there is no decision record (CMP-04) and no test suite (CMP-07), neither error would be detected by the firm before an examiner or a look-back found it. Severity would drop to a documentation gap if the calling job already scopes the input to one person, one business day and currency transactions only, which this review could not see; that is raised as an open question for Morgan.

fix.diff:
- def aggregate_daily(transactions):
-     total = 0
-     for txn in transactions:
-         total = total + txn["amount"]
-     return total
+ def aggregate_currency_by_direction(transactions, person_id, business_day):
+     """Return (cash_in, cash_out) for one person over one business day.
+
+     Aggregation entity is the person, not the account: 31 CFR 1010.313(b) aggregates
+     transactions by or on behalf of any person. TO-VERIFY.
+     """
+     cash_in = cash_out = 0
+     for txn in transactions:
+         if txn["instrument"] != "currency":
+             continue
+         if txn["person_id"] != person_id or txn["business_day"] != business_day:
+             continue
+         if txn["direction"] == "in":
+             cash_in += txn["amount"]
+         else:
+             cash_out += txn["amount"]
+     return cash_in, cash_out
fix.why: It makes the three qualifiers the rule states into explicit, reviewable code: direction is kept separate so either leg can breach on its own, the entity is the person the rule names, and non-currency activity is excluded rather than silently counted. The reportability test then becomes cash_in > threshold or cash_out > threshold, which is the rule as written. The signature also documents the aggregation contract, so the next reader cannot assume a scoping that the caller may not provide.

title: The decision is a bare bool: no inputs, computed total, threshold applied or timestamp is recorded, so no reporting decision can be reconstructed
location: alert_threshold_check.py:17-19 (is_reportable returns a bool), :9-14 (the computed total is discarded on return)
standard: CLAUDE.md section 4: detection rules must be explainable and auditable with deterministic inputs and a traceable link from alert to logic to obligation. BSA record retention, 31 CFR 1010.430, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-D/section-1010.430 . CTR filing deadline 31 CFR 1010.306(a)(1), TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.306
problem: Line 19 returns the result of a comparison and nothing else. The computed total from aggregate_daily is discarded. The module contains no logging, no return of the evidence, no record of which transactions were considered, no threshold value or version, no entity identifier, no window, and no timestamp. There is nothing persisted for a positive decision and nothing at all for a negative one.
likely_cause: The function was designed as a pure predicate, which is good engineering style and wrong for a regulated decision. In detection logic the reasoning is the deliverable, not a by-product, and nobody asked what evidence the decision needed to leave behind.
impact: Why an account did or did not alert on a given day cannot be reconstructed after the fact from anything this code produces. Three practical consequences follow. A look-back or model-validation exercise cannot perform below-the-line testing, because non-alerting days leave no total to compare against a lowered threshold. A challenge to a specific filing or non-filing cannot be answered with evidence of what the system actually computed. And because the threshold is overridable per call (CMP-02) and unversioned (CMP-08), even the value in force at the time of a past decision is unrecoverable. Record retention expectations under the BSA assume the supporting record exists; here none is created, so retention has nothing to retain.

fix.diff:
- def is_reportable(transactions, limit=DAILY_LIMIT):
-     return aggregate_daily(transactions) > limit
+ def evaluate_reportability(transactions, person_id, business_day, threshold=None):
+     """Return a decision record, not a bare bool."""
+     applied = CTR_THRESHOLD_USD if threshold is None else threshold
+     cash_in, cash_out = aggregate_currency_by_direction(transactions, person_id, business_day)
+     return {
+         "reportable": cash_in > applied or cash_out > applied,
+         "cash_in": cash_in,
+         "cash_out": cash_out,
+         "threshold_applied": applied,
+         "threshold_version": CTR_THRESHOLD_VERSION,
+         "threshold_overridden": threshold is not None,
+         "person_id": person_id,
+         "business_day": business_day,
+         "txn_count_considered": len(transactions),
+         "rule_id": "REQ-CTR-001",
+         "evaluated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
+     }
fix.why: It makes the decision self-evidencing, so the record that an auditor or a look-back needs is produced by the control itself rather than reconstructed later from code that may since have changed. Emitting the record for negative decisions as well as positive ones is what makes below-the-line testing possible at all. Recording threshold_applied and threshold_overridden closes the gap CMP-02 opens, because the value actually used is captured at the moment it is used.

title: Alerting threshold sits exactly on the statutory reporting threshold, leaving no margin and no structuring coverage; the > boundary itself is correct
standard: 31 CFR 1010.311, filing required for a currency transaction of more than $10,000, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.311 . Structuring prohibition 31 USC 5324, TO-VERIFY: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/5324 , and 31 CFR 1010.314, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.314
problem: On the boundary question, stated plainly because it is the one thing the code gets right: strict greater-than at line 19 against a limit of 10000 matches more than $10,000 as the rule is worded, so a day totalling exactly $10,000.00 is correctly not reported. Using >= would over-report. No change is needed there. The design weakness is separate. Setting the detection threshold identical to the statutory reporting threshold gives the control zero margin, and it makes the rule structurally blind to structuring, because structuring consists of deliberately keeping same-day activity below $10,000 and this rule cannot fire below $10,000 by construction. Nothing else in the file or the project provides that coverage; there is exactly one Python file.
likely_cause: The reporting threshold and the alerting threshold were treated as the same thing. They serve different purposes: one is a deterministic filing trigger fixed by rule, the other is a risk-based detection parameter that should be tuned.
impact: Two gaps. First, no tolerance for data imperfection: a rounding difference, a late-posting item, a missing feed record or an FX conversion error on a genuinely reportable day pushes the total under the line and the day is silently not reported, with nothing recorded to show it was close (see CMP-04). Second, a coverage gap on structuring, which is the predicate typology this threshold most directly invites. A person depositing $9,500 on consecutive days never trips this rule. A firm relying on this code alone would have a CTR trigger and no structuring detection.

fix.diff:
# Keep the CTR filing trigger exactly on the rule: strictly greater than $10,000.
  CTR_THRESHOLD_USD = 10000

+ # Separate, risk-based near-threshold band for investigation. Not a filing trigger.
+ # Rationale: margin for data imperfection plus structuring typology coverage.
+ # Owner / set / last tuned / next review: <to be completed>. Version: v1.
+ NEAR_THRESHOLD_FLOOR_USD = 9000
+
+ # Separate scenario, not this module: multi-day structuring over a rolling window.
fix.why: It splits the two controls that are currently one. The filing trigger stays exactly on the rule text, so reporting stays correct. The near-threshold band becomes a tunable detection parameter with its own governance record, which is what gives the control margin and makes below-the-line testing meaningful. Structuring needs a rolling multi-day window and belongs in its own scenario; naming that here records the gap rather than leaving it invisible.

title: Threshold and transaction amounts carry no currency, no unit and no FX treatment
location: alert_threshold_check.py:6 (bare integer 10000), :13 (txn["amount"] consumed with no currency check), :11 (total initialised as an untyped integer)
standard: 31 CFR 1010.311 expresses the threshold in US dollars, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.311 . CLAUDE.md section 4, explainable and auditable thresholds with documented meaning.
problem: Line 6 is the bare integer 10000. Nothing states the currency, and nothing states the unit, so the value is equally readable as 10000 dollars or 10000 cents. Line 13 adds txn["amount"] with no currency field consulted and no conversion applied, so amounts in different currencies would be added together as if they were the same unit. There is no FX rate, no rate date and no rounding policy anywhere in the module.
likely_cause: A single-currency, whole-dollar deployment was assumed and the assumption was never written down. Monetary values are also commonly held in minor units upstream, and nothing here rules that out.
impact: If amounts arrive in cents, the effective threshold is $100 and the rule over-reports by two orders of magnitude. If amounts arrive in mixed currencies, the total is arithmetically meaningless and reportability is wrong in an unpredictable direction. Neither failure is visible from the code, and neither would be caught, because there is no decision record showing the total (CMP-04) and no test asserting the unit (CMP-07). The CTR threshold is a US dollar figure, so a currency-blind aggregate cannot be evidenced as applying it.

fix.diff:
- DAILY_LIMIT = 10000
+ CTR_THRESHOLD_USD = Decimal("10000.00")  # USD, whole dollars and cents

  for txn in transactions:
+     if txn["currency"] != "USD":
+         raise ValueError(
+             f"non-USD amount reached the CTR aggregate: {txn['currency']}; "
+             "convert at the transaction-date rate upstream and record the rate used"
+         )
      total = total + txn["amount"]
fix.why: Naming the currency in the identifier and using Decimal removes both ambiguities at the point of definition and prevents binary float error accumulating near the boundary, which matters because the boundary is exact. Refusing a non-USD amount outright is the safe default: it converts a silent wrong answer into a loud failure. Conversion belongs upstream where the rate and rate date can be recorded alongside the converted value, so the decision record can evidence it.

title: No tests exist for detection logic, so control effectiveness cannot be evidenced
location: alert_threshold_check.py:1-19 (whole module); no test file anywhere in /tmp/vsit-eval-process-plugin-mode-open-4ac_cr0e/proj
standard: CLAUDE.md section 4: tests are mandatory for rule logic, known true-positive and false-positive cases. Definition of Done, Tested item: detection logic requires true-positive and false-positive cases. FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual expectation that monitoring systems are validated and periodically tested, TO-VERIFY: https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/manual
problem: The project contains exactly one Python file, the module under review. There is no test file, no test directory, no test framework configuration and no recorded test command. The detection logic therefore has neither a true-positive case nor a false-positive case, and the exact boundary at $10,000.00, which is where the rule text and the code most easily diverge, is unasserted.
likely_cause: The module is small enough to look self-evidently correct. Its actual behaviour depends on three unstated assumptions about direction, entity and currency, none of which a reader can check without a test that pins them.
impact: Stating the regulatory consequence rather than the engineering one: the firm has no evidence that this control operates as intended, and cannot produce any at examination. Every defect in CMP-03, CMP-05 and CMP-06 would have been caught by a first-pass test pair, which is direct evidence that the absence of tests is what allowed them to persist. It also means no regression barrier: a future change to the aggregation or the threshold could alter reporting outcomes with nothing to detect it. The Tested item of the Definition of Done is not met, and because execution consent is withheld for this engagement, even tests written now could only be authored and not run, so the best attainable state remains DoD PARTIAL.

fix.diff:
+ # tests/test_alert_threshold_check.py
+ def test_true_positive_above_threshold():
+     assert is_reportable([{"amount": 10000.01}]) is True
+
+ def test_false_positive_exactly_at_threshold():
+     # 31 CFR 1010.311 says MORE THAN $10,000; exactly $10,000 is not reportable.
+     assert is_reportable([{"amount": 10000}]) is False
+
+ def test_false_positive_opposing_directions_must_not_be_summed():
+     # $9,000 in and $9,000 out is not a reportable day under 31 CFR 1010.313(b).
+     ...
+
+ def test_true_positive_aggregated_across_one_person_two_accounts():
+     ...
fix.why: The first two pin the boundary in both directions, which is the single assertion most likely to prevent a real reporting error. The second pair encodes the aggregation rule's own qualifiers as executable expectations, so CMP-03 cannot silently regress once fixed. All fixtures are synthetic amounts with no identifiers, so the suite satisfies section 5 by construction. Record the exact command used to run them; do not assume a framework the project has not chosen.

title: No change control over the detection logic or the threshold: no repository, no version, no approval record
location: alert_threshold_check.py:1-19 (whole module); project root has no .git directory
standard: CLAUDE.md section 4: all detection-logic changes need review before merge by code-reviewer and compliance-reviewer, and hard-coded thresholds require a recorded rationale and tuning date. FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual expectation of documented change control over monitoring rules and thresholds, TO-VERIFY: https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/manual
problem: The project root contains no .git directory, verified directly. There is therefore no commit history, no authorship, no commit message, no branch, no pull request and no merge approval for this file. The threshold at line 6 carries no version identifier, so successive values cannot be distinguished. No approval record, no effective date and no prior review evidence exists anywhere in the project. This is reported as observed absence; the review draws no inference about whether the file is new or long-standing, because nothing on disk supports either conclusion.
likely_cause: The file was written outside any version-controlled workflow, most likely as a quick utility that was never promoted into one. Change control is usually inherited from the repository, so a file that never entered one never acquired it.
impact: The regulatory consequence, not the engineering one: the firm cannot demonstrate that its currency-transaction detection logic was reviewed and approved before use, cannot show when the threshold took effect or who authorised it, and cannot reconstruct which version of the rule produced any past reporting decision. Combined with CMP-04, which creates no decision record, there is no path at all from a historical filing or non-filing back to the logic that produced it. A look-back exercise could not establish the rule in force on a given date. This also makes the threshold review cycle unenforceable, since there is no record of when the last review occurred.

fix.diff:
+ Place the module under version control before it governs any reporting decision:
+   git init && git add alert_threshold_check.py && git commit
+ Commit message records: the obligation implemented, the threshold value, its rationale,
+ its effective date, the named owner, and the code-reviewer plus compliance-reviewer sign-off.
+
+ In the module, version the threshold explicitly:
+ CTR_THRESHOLD_VERSION = "v1"  # bump on every value change; recorded in each decision record
fix.why: Version control supplies the authorship, date and approval trail that section 4 requires and that no comment can substitute for, because a comment can be edited without trace. An explicit threshold version carried into the decision record (CMP-04) is what lets a past decision be tied to the exact parameter set that produced it, which is the specific thing a look-back needs and cannot currently obtain.

title: The module conflates a mandatory CTR filing trigger with a discretionary investigation alert
location: alert_threshold_check.py:1 (docstring: used by the alerting job to decide whether a candidate is reportable), :10 (Total the value of a day's transactions), :18 (breaches the reporting limit), :17 (function named is_reportable)
standard: 31 CFR 1010.311, mandatory CTR filing, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.311 . Suspicious activity reporting for banks, 31 CFR 1020.320, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1020/subpart-C/section-1020.320 . CLAUDE.md section 4, explainable detection logic.
problem: Line 1 places the module inside an alerting job, while lines 17 and 18 name its output reportable and describe it as breaching the reporting limit. Those are two different things. A CTR determination under 31 CFR 1010.311 is mandatory, deterministic and dictated by the rule. An alert is a risk-based prompt for human investigation that may or may not lead to a filing. The artifact never says which of the two it produces, and the same bare bool is consumed for whichever it is.
likely_cause: The threshold is shared between the two purposes, so the distinction between triggering a filing and raising an alert was never forced into the design.
impact: If the bool drives a filing, then the defects in CMP-03, CMP-05 and CMP-06 translate directly into failures to file or unnecessary filings, and the 15-calendar-day filing clock under 31 CFR 1010.306(a)(1) starts from an event this code cannot evidence. If instead it raises an alert for review, the same defects translate into investigation coverage gaps, which is serious but different in kind and in remediation. Because the artifact does not distinguish them, neither the reviewer nor a future maintainer can tell which risk applies, and the correct severity of three other findings depends on the answer. This is raised as an open question for Morgan to put to the user.

fix.diff:
"""Small utility used by the alerting job to decide whether a candidate is reportable.
+
+ PURPOSE: <choose one and state it>
+   (a) CTR filing determination under 31 CFR 1010.311. Mandatory and deterministic.
+       Output drives a filing; errors are reporting failures.
+   (b) Investigation alert. Risk-based prompt for human review; a filing may not follow.
+ The two must not share one output. If both are needed, return them as distinct fields.
  """
fix.why: Naming the purpose in the artifact fixes which obligation governs it, which in turn fixes the tolerance for error, the required evidence and the escalation path. It costs nothing and removes an ambiguity that currently sits underneath three other findings. Where both outputs are genuinely needed, separating them in the decision record keeps the deterministic filing trigger from being tuned as if it were a risk parameter.

title: The aggregation window is described only as a day, with no definition of business day, timezone or cut-off
location: alert_threshold_check.py:9 (aggregate_daily), :10 (docstring: a day's transactions), :6 (DAILY_LIMIT names a day it never defines)
standard: 31 CFR 1010.313(b) aggregates over any one business day, TO-VERIFY: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-C/section-1010.313 . CLAUDE.md section 4, deterministic inputs.
problem: The word daily appears in the constant name at line 6 and in the function name at line 9, and the docstring at line 10 says a day's transactions, but the module never defines the window. It takes no date argument, applies no date filter and states no timezone or cut-off. As the reviewer reads the aggregation provision, it speaks of one business day, which is not the same as a calendar day. Nothing in the artifact says which is intended, and the SME guidance on under-alerting names aggregation windows and period boundaries as a recurring cause of missed activity. Ravi owns the engineering defect that no date filtering happens at all; this finding is the separate question of which window the rule requires and how it is defined.
likely_cause: The window was assumed to be imposed by the caller and the definition was left to whatever the upstream job happens to use. Timezone and cut-off questions usually surface only when activity lands near midnight.
impact: Activity split across a boundary that the deployed definition draws differently from the rule is never summed over the line, so a reportable day can be missed. A calendar-day window over a weekend or holiday period, or a posting-date window where the rule looks to the business day, shifts which transactions fall together. The effect is invisible because no decision record shows the window evaluated (CMP-04) and no test pins it (CMP-07). Severity stays medium rather than higher only because the window may in fact be correctly imposed upstream, which this review could not see.

fix.diff:
- def aggregate_daily(transactions):
-     """Total the value of a day's transactions for one account."""
+ def aggregate_business_day(transactions, business_day):
+     """Total currency transactions for one BUSINESS day, per 31 CFR 1010.313(b). TO-VERIFY.
+
+     business_day is the institution's posting business day in <named timezone>, with the
+     cut-off defined in <named source>. It is NOT a calendar day: weekends and bank holidays
+     roll forward. Callers must supply it; this function never infers it.
+     """
fix.why: Making the window an explicit required argument stops it being an unstated assumption that differs between callers, and it becomes a value the decision record can capture. Writing the timezone and cut-off into the docstring means the boundary case is defined in one place that a tester and an examiner can both read, instead of being discovered through a missed filing.

title: Applicable obligation set cannot be closed without three answers only the user can give
location: alert_threshold_check.py:1-19 (whole module; the questions concern its deployment context, which is not in the artifact)
standard: CLAUDE.md section 2, regulatory scope must be established rather than assumed. Definition of Done, Open questions dispositioned item: every open question is formally closed by its owner.

Question two in particular is the live risk: if Part 504 applies, threshold governance carries a formal annual review and certification duty, which makes CMP-02 materially more serious than its current critical framing on federal grounds alone. fix.diff:

+   Q1. Does is_reportable drive a CTR filing, or raise an alert for investigation?

fix.why: Each answer resolves a specific severity that is currently carrying an assumption, so recording them turns three provisional gradings into evidenced ones. Putting them in the decision log rather than leaving them in prose is what lets the Open questions dispositioned item be met at the gate.
